techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing trains a model so that its predictions carry as little information as possible about a protected attribute, such as sex or race. Two neural networks are trained together, a predictor that learns the main task, such as estimating default risk, and an adversary that tries to guess each person's protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is updated to stay accurate while making the adversary's guesses fail, which pushes its outputs towards equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups (demographic parity). If the adversary is also given the true label, the predictor is penalised only for information about the attribute beyond what the label carries, which targets equal error rates across groups (equalised odds). The method needs the protected attribute for every training example and a model trained by gradient descent.

example_use_cases.description: A technology company trains a CV-screening model with an adversary that tries to guess each applicant's gender from the model's shortlisting score, so that selection rates come out similar for men and women (demographic parity) instead of leaning on CV features that happen to correlate with gender.

A lender trains a default-risk model for loan approvals with an adversary that is given each applicant's score and true repayment outcome and tries to guess their age band, so that false-positive and false-negative rates are similar across age bands (equalised odds) while predictive accuracy is kept.

A hospital group trains a COVID-19 screening model on emergency-department data with an adversary that tries to guess patient ethnicity from the model's score and the true test result, so that error rates are similar across ethnic groups while screening performance stays clinically useful.

limitations.description: The adversary only sees what it is given, usually the predictor's score and, for equalised odds, the true label. The method therefore targets one output-level criterion and gives no assurance that hidden layers are free of protected-attribute information, or that a different criterion holds.
Needs the protected attribute for every training example, so it cannot be used where that attribute was never collected or may not be held.

Demographic parity and equalised odds generally cannot both be met, so one must be chosen before training. Equal error rates can also come from worsening one group's rates: in the original Adult income experiment, the false-positive rate for women rose from 0.025 to 0.065.

Training two networks against each other is unstable. The weight given to the adversary has to be tuned (adversary_loss_weight in AIF360), and a wrong setting can make training diverge or leave the result closer to a different criterion than the one intended.

The paper's guarantee that outputs meet the chosen criterion holds only if both networks converge and the adversary is strong enough. A weak adversary leaves bias in place, and the convexity assumptions behind the proof do not hold for typical neural networks, so fairness has to be checked on held-out data after training.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance, and its accuracy is within the agreed margin of the unconstrained model.
The default-risk model's false-positive and false-negative rates differ between age bands by no more than the agreed tolerance on held-out data.
The COVID-19 screening model's error rates are similar across ethnic groups in each external hospital cohort, with negative predictive value above the clinical threshold set for screening.
Compared with the same model trained without the adversary, the model's gap on the chosen fairness criterion is smaller on held-out data, at a reported cost in accuracy.

techniques.name: Prejudice Remover Regulariser
techniques.description: An in-processing fairness technique that adds a fairness penalty to machine learning models to reduce bias against protected groups. The method works by minimising 'mutual information' - essentially reducing how much the model's predictions reveal about sensitive attributes like race or gender. By adding this penalty term to the learning objective (typically in logistic regression), the technique ensures predictions become less dependent on protected features. This addresses not only direct discrimination but also indirect bias through correlated features. Practitioners can adjust a tuning parameter to balance between maintaining accuracy and removing prejudice from the model.

example_use_cases.description: Training credit scoring models with prejudice remover regularisation to ensure loan approval decisions are not influenced by gender or ethnicity, minimising mutual information between predictions and protected attributes whilst maintaining accurate risk assessment.

limitations.description: Requires careful tuning of the fairness penalty hyperparameter, where too high values severely degrade accuracy whilst too low values provide insufficient bias mitigation.
Primarily applicable to probabilistic discriminative models like logistic regression, limiting its use with other model architectures such as deep neural networks or tree-based methods.
Computational complexity increases with the calculation of mutual information between predictions and sensitive attributes, particularly for high-dimensional data.
May not fully eliminate all forms of discrimination, particularly when complex interactions between multiple sensitive attributes create intersectional biases.
Effectiveness depends on accurate identification and inclusion of all sensitive attributes, potentially missing hidden biases from unobserved protected characteristics.

resources.title: Fairness-Aware Classifier with Prejudice Remover Regularizer
Fairness in credit scoring: Assessment, implementation and profit implications
resources.abstract: The rise of algorithmic decision-making has spawned much research on fair machine learning (ML). Financial institutions use ML for building risk scorecards that support a range of credit-related decisions. Yet, the literature on fair ML in credit scoring is scarce. The paper makes three contributions. First, we revisit statistical fairness criteria and examine their adequacy for credit scoring. Second, we catalog algorithmic options for incorporating fairness goals in the ML model development pipeline. Last, we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data. The empirical results substantiate the evaluation of fairness measures, identify suitable options to implement fair credit scoring, and clarify the profit-fairness trade-off in lending decisions. We find that multiple fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once and recommend separation as a proper criterion for measuring the fairness of a scorecard. We also find fair in-processors to deliver a good balance between profit and fairness and show that algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at a relatively low cost. The codes corresponding to the paper are available on GitHub.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

sample_claims.text: The model's loan approval predictions reveal minimal statistical information about applicants' protected demographic characteristics
The hiring system's candidate evaluations are statistically independent of gender and ethnicity identifiers

techniques.name: Meta Fair Classifier
techniques.description: The meta fair classifier is a general-purpose training algorithm for fair classification. The user chooses a fairness metric, such as the statistical rate (each group's share of favourable outcomes) or the false discovery rate (the share of positive predictions that are wrong), and a target between 0 and 1 for how close to equal the groups' values must be. From labelled training examples that include the protected attribute, the algorithm fits a model of the data, solves a series of constrained optimisation problems, and returns the most accurate classifier that meets the target. It trains a new classifier rather than adjusting an existing one. The original paper proves the result comes close to the best classifier that meets the target, up to the error in the fitted model of the data.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment platform trains a shortlisting classifier with a statistical-rate target of 0.8, so that the selection rate for any gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate, and measures how much accuracy it gives up to reach that target.

A probation service building a recidivism risk classifier constrains false discovery rate parity, so that among people flagged as high risk, the share who do not go on to reoffend is similar across racial groups.

A hospital building a classifier for heart conditions constrains false discovery rate parity, so that false alarms, which send people for unnecessary medical attention, do not fall more heavily on women than on men.

limitations.description: It is a self-contained learner, not a wrapper. It cannot adjust a model you already run, and the paper lists extension to other classifier types as future work. It also needs the protected attribute for every training example, and teams must be willing to replace their model with the one it produces.

The AIF360 implementation supports only statistical rate and false discovery rate, and raises an error for any other metric. The paper's framework covers more, but other criteria, such as equalised odds, mean extra implementation work or choosing a different technique.

The guarantee depends on how well the fitted model of the data matches the real distribution, and the paper's bound carries error terms for any mismatch. In its experiments, a simple fitted model gave lower accuracy than competing methods at the same fairness level.
Results can vary from run to run. In a credit-scoring comparison, repeated runs sometimes missed the fairness target, which made averaging the results unusable.

The method solves a separate constrained optimisation problem for each value on a grid set by the tolerance, and the number multiplies for each additional fairness metric constrained at once. Combining several criteria quickly makes training slow.

resources.title: Classification with Fairness Constraints
resources.abstract: Developing classification algorithms that are fair with respect to sensitive attributes of the data is an important problem due to the increased deployment of classification algorithms in societal contexts. Several recent works have focused on studying classification with respect to specific fairness metrics, modeled the corresponding fair classification problem as constrained optimization problems, and developed tailored algorithms to solve them. Despite this, there still remain important metrics for which there are no fair classifiers with theoretical guarantees; primarily because the resulting optimization problem is non-convex. The main contribution of this paper is a meta-algorithm for classification that can take as input a general class of fairness constraints with respect to multiple non-disjoint and multi-valued sensitive attributes, and which comes with provable guarantees. In particular, our algorithm can handle non-convex "linear fractional" constraints (which includes fairness constraints such as predictive parity) for which no prior algorithm was known. Key to our results is an algorithm for a family of classification problems with convex constraints along with a reduction from classification problems with linear fractional constraints to this family. Empirically, we observe that our algorithm is fast, can achieve near-perfect fairness with respect to various fairness metrics, and the loss in accuracy due to the imposed fairness constraints is often small.

resources.title: Algorithmic decision making methods for fair credit scoring
resources.abstract: The effectiveness of machine learning in evaluating the creditworthiness of loan applicants has been demonstrated for a long time. However, there is concern that the use of automated decision-making processes may result in unequal treatment of groups or individuals, potentially leading to discriminatory outcomes. This paper seeks to address this issue by evaluating the effectiveness of 12 leading bias mitigation methods across 5 different fairness metrics, as well as assessing their accuracy and potential profitability for financial institutions. Through our analysis, we have identified the challenges associated with achieving fairness while maintaining accuracy and profitabiliy, and have highlighted both the most successful and least successful mitigation methods. Ultimately, our research serves to bridge the gap between experimental machine learning and its practical applications in the finance industry.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting classifier's selection rate for each gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate.
Among people the recidivism model flags as high risk, the share who do not reoffend differs between racial groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.

techniques.name: Exponentiated Gradient Reduction
techniques.description: Exponentiated gradient reduction trains a classifier that satisfies a chosen fairness criterion, such as demographic parity (equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups) or equalised odds (equal error rates across groups), while keeping error as low as it can. It reduces the problem to a series of ordinary training runs on the same data, each with different example weights. Between runs, a multiplicative update, the exponentiated gradient step, increases the weight on fairness constraints that are currently violated, and a standard classifier is retrained on the reweighted data. The output is a randomised classifier, a weighted mix of the classifiers trained along the way, with one drawn at random for each prediction. The original paper proves that its error and its fairness violation come close to the best achievable, up to a tolerance the user sets and the statistical error from a finite training set.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment team trains a shortlisting model under a demographic parity constraint so that selection rates are equal across gender groups, and sweeps the method's tolerance setting to see how much accuracy each step towards equality costs.

A justice agency building a recidivism risk model trains a logistic regression under a demographic parity constraint on race, then compares accuracy and fairness metrics against the unconstrained model on the same data before deciding whether to deploy it.

A lender trying equalised odds, true-positive-rate difference and demographic parity as constraints on its credit-scoring model picks the one that gives the best balance of accuracy and profit on its own data, since the best choice differs between datasets.

limitations.description: The guarantees assume the base learner can solve each weighted training problem close to exactly. Real learners only approximate this, so the stated bounds on error and fairness violation are approximate in practice. The learner must also accept per-example weights, which rules out some model types.

The result is a randomised mix of classifiers, so the same input can receive different predictions on repeat requests. This is hard to defend where decisions must be repeatable, as in appeals or audits.

Needs the protected attribute for every training example, although not at prediction time. It enforces one fairness criterion at a time, and the original paper leaves trading off several criteria as an open problem.

Each round retrains the base model, and the number of rounds needed grows with the square of the inverse of the tolerance, so halving the tolerance roughly quadruples training cost. Large datasets or slow models make tight tolerances expensive.

Constraint violation is controlled only up to sampling error, which is larger for small groups. In one credit-scoring comparison the best-performing constraint differed between datasets, so the right criterion has to be found by experiment on the data in hand.

resources.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
resources.abstract: We present a systematic approach for achieving fairness in a binary classification setting. While we focus on two well-known quantitative definitions of fairness, our approach encompasses many other previously studied definitions as special cases. The key idea is to reduce fair classification to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems, whose solutions yield a randomized classifier with the lowest (empirical) error subject to the desired constraints. We introduce two reductions that work for any representation of the cost-sensitive classifier and compare favorably to prior baselines on a variety of data sets, while overcoming several of their disadvantages.

This paper seeks to address this issue by evaluating the effectiveness of 12 leading bias mitigation methods across 5 different fairness metrics, as well as assessing their accuracy and potential profitability for financial institutions. resources.title: A fairness-focused approach to recidivism prediction: implications for accuracy, trust, and equity
resources.abstract: Fairness in AI has emerged as a critical priority, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice, where algorithmic decisions profoundly affect individuals and demographic groups. This study addresses persistent challenges of bias in recidivism prediction by evaluating the integrated application of fairness-enhancing techniques across the AI pipeline. Specifically, we analyze the integrated use of Reweighing, Adversarial Learning, Disparate Impact Remover, Exponentiated Gradient Reduction, Reject Option Classification, and Equalized Odds optimization. These methods are assessed using key fairness metrics, Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Predictive Equality Difference (PED), on two real-world recidivism datasets: COMPAS, a well-known publicly available dataset, and RisCanvi, a curated English dataset derived from a publicly available Spanish dataset. Our findings reveal trade-offs between fairness improvements and predictive accuracy, with fairness performance varying across integrated mitigation strategies. While individual techniques often fall short of effectively reducing bias, their integration across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages demonstrates a more comprehensive and robust capacity to address fairness concerns. In some instances, fairness mitigation strategies exacerbate disparities instead of reducing them, highlighting the complexity of achieving equitable AI outcomes. Some methods struggle with specific datasets, leading to worsened SPD, DI, EOD, or PED values, potentially reinforcing biases rather than eliminating them. Using multi-objective and bi-objective optimization frameworks, we identify optimal configurations that balance fairness and accuracy, contributing to a deeper understanding of fairness–accuracy trade-offs in AI systems. This study makes a novel contribution by systematically evaluating multi-phase fairness integration in recidivism prediction, bridging critical gaps in the literature. However, our results also underscore the risks of ineffective or counterproductive fairness interventions when not carefully tailored. Our findings highlight the necessity of tailoring bias mitigation strategies to specific datasets and contexts, providing actionable insights for developing equitable, diverse, and inclusive AI systems that are fair and reliable in the criminal justice system.

sample_claims.text: The lending model satisfies demographic parity constraints with quantifiable bounds on both error rate and fairness violation
On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.
The recidivism model's true-positive and false-positive rates differ across racial groups by less than the agreed tolerance, and the accuracy cost against the unconstrained model is reported.
Across a sweep of tolerance settings, the model's error and fairness violation trace out a reported trade-off curve, and the deployed setting is justified from it.

techniques.name: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
techniques.description: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations (LAFTR) trains an encoder that turns each record into a representation, a vector of learned features, from which a protected attribute is hard to recover, so that models later built on that representation by other parties, including for prediction tasks not known in advance, also treat groups fairly. It was designed for a data owner who shares encoded data with downstream model builders and cannot control how they train. During training, the encoder, a decoder that reconstructs the input and a classifier for the original task play against an adversary network that tries to predict the protected attribute from the representation; the encoder is updated to defeat the adversary while keeping the information the other two need. The adversary's objective is matched to demographic parity, equalised odds or equal opportunity, and the authors prove that an optimal adversary's objective bounds that unfairness measure for any classifier trained on the representation (for the two error-rate measures the adversary also sees the labels used in training, so the attribute is hidden given the label, and the bound is with respect to those labels). The output is a frozen encoder, delivered with the accuracy and fairness of classifiers trained on top of it.

example_use_cases.description: A data marketplace that supplies customer records to advertisers wants assurance that the targeting models advertisers build will not show offers to men and women at different rates. It trains LAFTR with the demographic parity adversary, releases only the encoded features, and audits a sample of advertisers' models for the gap in positive rates and for how well a fresh classifier can recover gender from the released features.

A health insurer's data team shares encoded claims and prescription data with external analytics suppliers who build their own risk models. It trains LAFTR with an equalised-odds adversary on a comorbidity-risk task, with patients aged 70 or over as the protected group, then measures error-rate gaps for classifiers trained on held-out condition-prediction tasks, because fairness on those new tasks has to be measured rather than assumed.

A hospital imaging research group compares LAFTR with standard training for a chest X-ray triage classifier, with patient sex as the protected attribute and the model-selection rule fixed in advance, to decide whether debiasing the representation narrows the gap in error rates enough to justify its extra training cost.

limitations.description: The fairness bound holds only for an optimal adversary. A weak or under-trained adversary underestimates how much protected information the representation still carries, so downstream models can be less fair than training suggested; the authors report uneven results in places, which they attribute to unstable adversarial training. Audit downstream models directly, including with a fresh classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation.

Transfer to new tasks is not guaranteed for the error-rate criteria. The equalised-odds and equal-opportunity adversaries use the original task's labels, so fairness on a new task with different labels is an empirical result: in the paper's health-data experiment LAFTR was the fairest method on seven of ten transfer tasks, and the authors leave open which tasks transfer fairly.

As formulated, it handles one binary protected attribute and a binary task label; intersectional groups, several attributes or multi-class outcomes need an extension. Training needs the protected attribute and, for the error-rate criteria, the task labels. In the paper's experiments the encoder also took the protected attribute as input, so it is needed whenever new records are encoded; no results are reported without it.

Measured gains can be small in practice. MEDFAIR, a peer-reviewed benchmark of eleven bias-mitigation methods including LAFTR on medical imaging datasets, found the methods did not significantly improve fairness over standard training when trained and tested on the same task, including across datasets (it did not test transfer to new tasks), and that the model-selection criterion changed fairness results substantially. Compare against a standard model under a selection rule stated in advance.

Up to four networks (encoder, decoder, classifier, adversary) are trained against each other, with three weights balancing accuracy, reconstruction and fairness. The paper argues reconstruction is needed for transfer and used different weights for fair classification (accuracy 1, reconstruction 0) and for transfer (accuracy 0, reconstruction 1), so settings do not carry over. The 2018 reference code pins Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.9; reimplementations sit inside research benchmarks.

resources.title: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
resources.abstract: In this paper, we advocate for representation learning as the key to mitigating unfair prediction outcomes downstream. Motivated by a scenario where learned representations are used by third parties with unknown objectives, we propose and explore adversarial representation learning as a natural method of ensuring those parties act fairly. We connect group fairness (demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) to different adversarial objectives. Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

resources.title: MEDFAIR: Benchmarking Fairness for Medical Imaging
resources.abstract: A multitude of work has shown that machine learning-based medical diagnosis systems can be biased against certain subgroups of people. This has motivated a growing number of bias mitigation algorithms that aim to address fairness issues in machine learning. However, it is difficult to compare their effectiveness in medical imaging for two reasons. First, there is little consensus on the criteria to assess fairness. Second, existing bias mitigation algorithms are developed under different settings, e.g., datasets, model selection strategies, backbones, and fairness metrics, making a direct comparison and evaluation based on existing results impossible. In this work, we introduce MEDFAIR, a framework to benchmark the fairness of machine learning models for medical imaging. MEDFAIR covers eleven algorithms from various categories, nine datasets from different imaging modalities, and three model selection criteria. Through extensive experiments, we find that the under-studied issue of model selection criterion can have a significant impact on fairness outcomes; while in contrast, state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms do not significantly improve fairness outcomes over empirical risk minimization (ERM) in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. We evaluate fairness from various perspectives and make recommendations for different medical application scenarios that require different ethical principles. Our framework provides a reproducible and easy-to-use entry point for the development and evaluation of future bias mitigation algorithms in deep learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ys-zong/MEDFAIR.

sample_claims.text: Classifiers trained by external parties on the released representation show a demographic parity difference below the agreed threshold on every downstream task audited.

A classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation released under the demographic parity objective does no better than always predicting the majority group, within an agreed margin.
The fairness of downstream risk models built on the shared encoded data was measured on each new prediction task rather than assumed from the task the encoder was trained on.
Under a model-selection rule fixed in advance, the debiased imaging model narrows the gap in error rates between patient groups relative to standard training by a measured margin.

techniques.name: Multi-Accuracy Boosting
techniques.description: An in-processing fairness technique that employs boosting algorithms to improve accuracy uniformly across demographic groups by iteratively correcting errors where the model performs poorly for certain subgroups. The method uses a multi-calibration approach that trains weak learners to focus on prediction errors for underperforming groups, ensuring that no group experiences systematically worse accuracy. This iterative boosting process continues until accuracy parity is achieved across all groups whilst maintaining overall model performance.

example_use_cases.description: Training a medical diagnosis model that achieves equal accuracy across age, gender, and ethnicity groups by using boosting to specifically target prediction errors for underrepresented patient demographics, ensuring equitable healthcare outcomes for all populations.

Building a robust fraud detection system that maintains consistent accuracy across different customer segments by iteratively correcting errors where the model performs poorly for specific demographic or geographic groups, ensuring reliable fraud prevention across all user types.

Developing a transparent hiring algorithm that provides clear evidence of equal performance across candidate demographics by using multi-accuracy boosting to systematically address group-specific prediction errors, enabling auditable fair recruitment processes.

limitations.description: Requires identifying and defining relevant subgroups or error regions, which may be challenging when group boundaries are unclear or overlapping.
Could increase model complexity significantly as the boosting process adds multiple weak learners, potentially affecting interpretability and computational efficiency.
May overfit to training data if very granular corrections are made, particularly when subgroups are small or the boosting process continues for too many iterations.
Performance depends on the quality of subgroup identification, and may fail to achieve fairness if important demographic intersections are not properly captured.
Convergence to equal accuracy across groups is not guaranteed, especially when there are fundamental differences in data distributions between groups.

resources.title: mcboost: Multi-Calibration Boosting for R (package documentation)
resources.abstract:
Implements Multi-Calibration Boosting (2018) <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/hebert-johnson18a.html> and
    Multi-Accuracy Boosting (2019) <arXiv:1805.12317> for the multi-calibration of a machine learning models prediction.
    MCBoost' updates predictions for sub-groups in an iterative fashion in order to mitigate biases like poor calibration or large accuracy differences across subgroups.
    Multi-Calibration works best in scenarios where the underlying data & labels are unbiased, but resulting models are.
    This is often the case, e.g. when an algorithm fits a majority population while ignoring or under-fitting minority populations.

resources.title: mcboost: Multi-Calibration Boosting for R
resources.abstract: Given the increasing usage of automated prediction systems in the context of high-stakes decisions, a growing body of research focuses on methods for detecting and mitigating biases in algorithmic decision-making.One important framework to audit for and mitigate biases in predictions is that of Multi-Calibration, introduced by Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018).The underlying fairness notion, Multi-Calibration, promotes the idea of multi-group fairness and requires calibrated predictions not only for marginal populations, but also for subpopulations that may be defined by complex intersections of many attributes.A simpler variant of Multi-Calibration, referred to as Multi-Accuracy, requires unbiased predictions for large collections of subpopulations.Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018) proposed a boosting-style algorithm for learning multi-calibrated predictors.Kim et al. (2019) demonstrated how to turn this algorithm into a post-processing strategy to achieve multi-accuracy, demonstrating empirical effectiveness across various domains.This package provides a stable implementation of the multi-calibration algorithm, called MCBoost.In contrast to other Fair ML approaches, MC-Boost does not harm the overall utility of a prediction model, but rather aims at improving calibration and accuracy for large sets of subpopulations post-training.MCBoost comes with strong theoretical guarantees, which have been explored formally in Hebert-Johnson et al.

resources.title: Multiaccuracy
resources.abstract: Prediction systems are successfully deployed in applications ranging from disease diagnosis, to predicting credit worthiness, to image recognition. Even when the overall accuracy is high, these systems may exhibit systematic biases that harm specific subpopulations; such biases may arise inadvertently due to underrepresentation in the data used to train a machine-learning model, or as the result of intentional malicious discrimination. We develop a rigorous framework of *multiaccuracy* auditing and post-processing to ensure accurate predictions across *identifiable subgroups*. Our algorithm, MULTIACCURACY-BOOST, works in any setting where we have black-box access to a predictor and a relatively small set of labeled data for auditing; importantly, this black-box framework allows for improved fairness and accountability of predictions, even when the predictor is minimally transparent. We prove that MULTIACCURACY-BOOST converges efficiently and show that if the initial model is accurate on an identifiable subgroup, then the post-processed model will be also. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach to improve the accuracy among minority subgroups in diverse applications (image classification, finance, population health). Interestingly, MULTIACCURACY-BOOST can improve subpopulation accuracy (e.g. for "black women") even when the sensitive features (e.g. "race", "gender") are not given to the algorithm explicitly.

resources.title: Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses
resources.abstract: As algorithms increasingly inform and influence decisions made about individuals, it becomes increasingly important to address concerns that these algorithms might be discriminatory. The output of an algorithm can be discriminatory for many reasons, most notably: (1) the data used to train the algorithm might be biased (in various ways) to favor certain populations over others; (2) the analysis of this training data might inadvertently or maliciously introduce biases that are not borne out in the data. This work focuses on the latter concern. We develop and study multicalbration -- a new measure of algorithmic fairness that aims to mitigate concerns about discrimination that is introduced in the process of learning a predictor from data. Multicalibration guarantees accurate (calibrated) predictions for every subpopulation that can be identified within a specified class of computations. We think of the class as being quite rich; in particular, it can contain many overlapping subgroups of a protected group. We show that in many settings this strong notion of protection from discrimination is both attainable and aligned with the goal of obtaining accurate predictions. Along the way, we present new algorithms for learning a multicalibrated predictor, study the computational complexity of this task, and draw new connections to computational learning models such as agnostic learning.

techniques.name: Fair Bayesian Optimisation
techniques.description: Fair Bayesian Optimisation (FairBO) tunes a model's hyperparameters, the settings fixed before training such as tree depth or regularisation strength, to find the most accurate model that also meets a fairness threshold chosen in advance, for example a difference in positive-prediction rates between two groups of at most 0.05. Because it only changes hyperparameters and retrains, it treats the model and its training pipeline as a black box, so it works with any model class and any group fairness metric, can enforce several metrics at once, and returns a model that need not use the protected attribute at prediction time (the attribute is still needed to measure fairness during the search). Each step trains a model with a candidate configuration and measures its validation accuracy and fairness, and two Gaussian processes (statistical models that predict a value together with its uncertainty) are fitted to the results of the configurations tried so far. The next configuration is the one with the highest expected improvement in accuracy weighted by the predicted probability of meeting the fairness constraint; until a fair configuration has been found, the search maximises that probability alone. The output is the best configuration that met the constraint, with its accuracy and fairness measurements.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team tunes a gradient-boosted credit-risk model under a constraint that the approval-rate difference between applicants of different nationality stays at or below 0.05. It records the most accurate configuration that met the constraint beside the result of unconstrained tuning, so the model approval committee can see what accuracy the constraint cost.

An HR analytics team at a large employer tunes a random forest that ranks job applications for interview, enforcing limits on the gender gap in true positive rates and on the gap in shortlisting rates at the same time, because its policy commits to both equal opportunity and comparable shortlisting rates.

A data science team at a health insurer already runs an adversarially debiased claims-triage model whose fairness changed sharply with its learning rate and adversary weight. It uses FairBO to tune those hyperparameters under a statistical parity constraint, rather than tuning them for accuracy alone and checking fairness afterwards.

A local authority building a model to prioritise benefit-fraud reviews cannot use ethnicity as an input at decision time. It holds ethnicity only in a validation extract, uses FairBO to select hyperparameters that keep the referral-rate gap within its equality impact assessment threshold, and then confirms the gap on a separate held-out sample before deployment.

limitations.description: It can only reach fairness that some hyperparameter setting already provides. If no configuration in the search space meets the threshold, it returns no fair model. The originating paper found that regularisation hyperparameters (tree depth, weight penalties, learning rate) have the largest effect on fairness, so a search space without them leaves fewer fair options.

The fairness metric and its threshold must be fixed before the search, and the result says nothing about metrics that were not constrained. Choosing them is a normative decision the method does not make. If decision-makers need to see the whole accuracy-fairness trade-off before picking a threshold, a multi-objective search is needed, which the paper found slower to reach a model meeting a given threshold.

A constraint can be met by a model that barely distinguishes between anyone. The paper argues that as regularisation grows, predictions approach a constant and satisfy every group fairness metric, and in its example run on the Adult dataset (random forest, parity gap at most 0.05) random search found fair models only at the accuracy of always predicting the majority class. Check accuracy and error rates within each group, not only the fairness gap, before accepting the result.

Every step trains a full model, so the cost is the training cost multiplied by the number of evaluations (the paper used up to 100), which is expensive for large models. The fairness value guiding the search is estimated on the validation split used during tuning, so it carries sampling error that is large when a group is small; confirm the gap on held-out data before relying on it.

It has little evidence behind it and no maintained implementation. The paper tests only binary classification with a binary protected attribute on three tabular datasets, leaving regression, image and language tasks to future work. The code shipped in AutoGluon 0.3.1 (2021) and was dropped in 0.4.0; Syne Tune moved it to a legacy folder in 0.14 and removed it in 0.15 (December 2025), though its documentation still describes it. Use means pinning an old release or rebuilding it.

resources.title: Fair Bayesian Optimization
resources.abstract: Given the increasing importance of machine learning (ML) in our lives, several algorithmic fairness techniques have been proposed to mitigate biases in the outcomes of the ML models. However, most of these techniques are specialized to cater to a single family of ML models and a specific definition of fairness, limiting their adaptibility in practice. We introduce a general constrained Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to optimize the performance of any ML model while enforcing one or multiple fairness constraints. BO is a model-agnostic optimization method that has been successfully applied to automatically tune the hyperparameters of ML models. We apply BO with fairness constraints to a range of popular models, including random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks, showing that we can obtain accurate and fair solutions by acting solely on the hyperparameters. We also show empirically that our approach is competitive with specialized techniques that enforce model-specific fairness constraints, and outperforms preprocessing methods that learn fair representations of the input data. Moreover, our method can be used in synergy with such specialized fairness techniques to tune their hyperparameters. Finally, we study the relationship between fairness and the hyperparameters selected by BO. We observe a correlation between regularization and unbiased models, explaining why acting on the hyperparameters leads to ML models that generalize well and are fair.
